section_summary: This section chiefly documents narcotics smuggling, opium addiction, and the government opium monopoly in Dairen and the Kwantung Leased Territory from 1935 through 1939. It includes lists of suspected traffickers, consular assessments of the illicit trade, detailed translations of Japanese opium-control ordinances, statistics on licensed addicts, and criticism of the monopoly’s substantial revenue and limited success in reducing addiction. The final pages contain 1930 regulations governing opium transportation aboard Japanese ships and correspondence about sensational newspaper claims that enormous quantities of cocaine were being advertised for sale in Japan.

subfiles.title: Conclusion of report on narcotics manufacture in Chinese localities
subfiles.about: Reports that military and local figures became involved in narcotics manufacture at several Chinese localities.
subfiles.summary: This concluding fragment names Generals Yui Kue-Chai and Cho Ming-Chi and Wang Feng-Min as figures associated with narcotics manufacture in their respective areas. Nicholson states that his agent is conducting a detailed investigation and expects to submit further facts.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Treasury Attaché Nicholson’s Dairen suspect list
subfiles.about: Transmits two copies of Nicholson’s September 23 report identifying suspected narcotics smugglers present in Dairen.
subfiles.summary: The Treasury Department forwards a confidential report from its Shanghai attaché. The enclosed report contains names and addresses of suspected smugglers who were in Dairen on September 15, 1935.

subfiles.title: Dairen Agent Report: smugglers and suspects
subfiles.from: M. R. Nicholson, Treasury attaché, Shanghai
subfiles.about: Lists the names and Dairen addresses of numerous suspected smugglers and narcotics associates.
subfiles.summary: The report supplies an extensive list of suspects located in Dairen on September 15, 1935, usually with a street, hotel, or district address. It identifies Igolkowsky, Shpraus, and Kobzareff as partners in the North-Manchuria Transport Company and associates them with Hatzopoulos, Gorfunkel, Leibovitz, Goldberg, and others. The author promises further lists.

subfiles.title: Effects of Recent Chinese Legislation on Drug Traffic
subfiles.from: Troy L. Perkins, American vice consul, Dairen
subfiles.about: Assesses the limited direct effect of Chinese drug laws on Japanese-administered Kwantung and summarizes opium revenue, imports, illicit trafficking, and addiction treatment.
subfiles.summary: Perkins explains that recent Chinese legislation has little direct application in the Kwantung Leased Territory, though China and increasingly Manchuria supply illicit drugs. Budget estimates show substantial monopoly revenue and expenditures, while customs returns record large 1934 opium imports through Dairen from Turkey, Egypt, Persia, and the Japanese Empire. Press reports and police activity indicate extensive illicit manufacture, sale, and transshipment beyond the official opium figures. The Dairen government home for addicts had treated about 5,000 people in ten years and estimated that three to four percent of the local population needed treatment.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Nanking despatch on Kwantung narcotics control
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to another file containing a despatch on narcotics control in the Kwantung Leased Territory.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references file 894C.01/84 and identifies a September 12, 1935 despatch from Nanking associated with Atcheson. Its subject is narcotics control in the Kwantung Leased Territory.

subfiles.title: Confidential transmittal of report on the Kwantung Leased Territory
subfiles.about: Sends a confidential copy of an August 19 report on Kwantung for the Commissioner of Narcotics.
subfiles.summary: The State Department forwards a report because of Kwantung’s unusual administrative position and its importance as a source for the illicit narcotics trade. It particularly directs attention to the report’s treatment of the territorial budget and narcotics control.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Treasury letter transmitting Nicholson reports
subfiles.about: Cross-references a Treasury Department letter transmitting copies of reports by Treasury Attaché Nicholson.
subfiles.summary: The file note points to file 893.114 Narcotics/1340. It records a November 6, 1935 Treasury letter concerning reports from Nicholson at Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Dairen despatch on Chinese narcotics legislation
subfiles.about: Forwards Dairen despatch No. 76 on the effect of recent Chinese legislation on narcotics traffic in Kwantung.
subfiles.summary: The Department encloses two confidential copies of the October 3, 1935 Dairen despatch for the Commissioner of Narcotics. The report concerns the effects of Chinese drug legislation in the Kwantung Leased Territory.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference concerning Harold S. Jones’s death
subfiles.about: Points to information concerning Harold S. Jones’s death at Dairen from morphine poisoning.
subfiles.summary: The file note cross-references file 311.113 Jones.Harold S./2. It identifies a November 8, 1935 letter containing information about Jones’s fatal morphine poisoning.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of material concerning Curt Smith and Max Kattwinkel
subfiles.from: Wayne C. Taylor, Assistant Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: Forwards a Paris Treasury attaché’s letter and enclosures about Curt Smith and Kattwinkel’s statement to German narcotics authorities.
subfiles.summary: The Treasury Department refers to earlier correspondence concerning Curt Smith’s suspected involvement in illicit narcotics traffic. It transmits two copies of the acting Treasury attaché’s September 19 letter and Kattwinkel’s August 28 statement before the German Central Narcotics Office in Berlin.

subfiles.title: Acting Treasury attaché’s transmittal of the Curt Smith memorandum
subfiles.from: J. Homer Butler, Acting Treasury Attaché, Paris
subfiles.about: Transmits Charles B. Dyar’s memorandum and a translation of Kattwinkel’s statement about Curt Smith.
subfiles.summary: Butler forwards Dyar’s September 14 memorandum on Smith’s suspected narcotics activities. He also encloses the translated statement of Smith’s former associate Max Kattwinkel and notes that copies were sent to Nicholson in Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Memorandum concerning Curt Smith and Kattwinkel
subfiles.from: Charles B. Dyar, Special Agent, Bureau of Narcotics
subfiles.about: Forwards Kattwinkel’s statement and discusses evidence that Smith’s transactions may have been commercial swindles.
subfiles.summary: Dyar refers to prior reports from Nicholson concerning Smith as a suspected trafficker. He encloses Kattwinkel’s statement, reports the German Central Narcotics Office’s view that the transactions may have been swindles, and notes that British authorities were asked to obtain evidence from injured merchants. The memorandum also mentions Berlin merchant Willy Stieler and his business connections.

subfiles.title: Statement of Max Friedrich Kattwinkel
subfiles.about: Describes Kattwinkel’s dealings with Curt Smith, alleges misuse of his firm and credit in fraudulent shipments, and denies any personal involvement in narcotics.
subfiles.summary: Kattwinkel recounts his career in China, his Nicaraguan consular appointment, and the development of business relations with Curt Smith. He says Smith used his power of attorney to draw approximately £12,000 against worthless or grossly overvalued merchandise shipped to Hong Kong and Dairen, with further shipments stopped before completion. Kattwinkel identifies intermediaries and maintains that the transactions were invoice swindles that harmed his reputation. He emphatically denies ever participating in narcotics transactions and offers his assistance to German authorities.

subfiles.title: Thompson warning on the Dairen narcotics-smuggling network
subfiles.from: Berger, transmitting a message from Beriah M. Thompson
subfiles.to: Secretary of State for the Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: Warns of a large European-operated narcotics-smuggling network based in Dairen and names shippers and routes requiring surveillance.
subfiles.summary: Thompson reports that cheap narcotics are available in unlimited quantities through a large Dairen racket operated by Europeans connected with shipping businesses. He recommends watching all vessels and cargoes originating at Dairen, especially soybean oil in cases or tanks, and lists several suspected shippers or agents. Ships calling at Newchwang and Hulutao are also singled out for inspection.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Thompson’s narcotics-smuggling telegram
subfiles.about: Forwards the Tientsin telegram containing Thompson’s report on illicit narcotics traffic in Korea, Manchuria, and Kwantung.
subfiles.summary: The State Department encloses two copies of the November 2 telegram from the American Consulate General at Tientsin. It identifies the embedded message as a report by retired Commander Beriah M. Thompson to the Treasury Secretary.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japan’s 1935 annual narcotics report
subfiles.about: Cross-references Japan’s annual report for 1935 under League of Nations document number C.541.M.350.1936.XI.
subfiles.summary: The file note points to file 894.114 Narcotics/252. It identifies the referenced item as Japan’s annual report for 1935.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report on A. Beerbrayer
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report from China concerning suspected trafficker A. Beerbrayer.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to file 811.111 Beerbrayer.A. It records a Treasury Department letter transmitting a report from China on Beerbrayer’s activities.

subfiles.title: Developments in the Opium Monopoly of the Kwantung Leased Territory
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, American consul, Dairen
subfiles.about: Explains new Kwantung opium laws, the conversion of the monopoly into a manufacturing enterprise, and doubts about whether tighter controls will reduce addiction.
subfiles.summary: Turner reports that Imperial Ordinance No. 84 and Kwantung Bureau Ordinance No. 8 centralize the manufacture of prepared opium in the Kwantung Monopoly Bureau and tighten controls on dealers, permits, and addicts. Director Noboru Yasunaga argues that the new Port Arthur factory and stricter rules will eliminate abuses and ultimately reduce addiction. Turner acknowledges that the machinery permits better control but questions whether the government will sacrifice lucrative opium revenue, noting experience in Korea and Taiwan, attractive monopoly packaging, generous retailer profits, and the open availability of bootleg opium. He proposes later reports on the factory and government sanitarium.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 84 and Kwantung Bureau Ordinance No. 7
subfiles.from: Japanese government; translated by William T. Turner
subfiles.about: Amends the Kwantung opium law to establish official manufacture and stricter possession rules and orders the amendments into force.
subfiles.summary: Imperial Ordinance No. 84 assigns the sale, dispensing, and manufacture of prepared and medicinal opium to the authorities. It prohibits retail dealers from processing or adulterating opium and prescribes imprisonment and fines for unauthorized manufacture, possession, or consumption. The accompanying Bureau Ordinance No. 7 places the amendments in force on February 21, 1938, under Ambassador Kenkichi Ueda.

subfiles.title: Kwantung Bureau Ordinance No. 8: Rules for Enforcement of the Opium Law
subfiles.from: Kwantung Bureau; translated by William T. Turner
subfiles.to: Kwantung authorities, opium dealers, medical professionals, and permitted smokers
subfiles.about: Sets comprehensive rules for licensing smokers, distributing opium, regulating dealers, maintaining records, reporting transactions, and punishing violations.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance requires adult Manchurian or Chinese addicts to obtain certificates specifying their dosage and designated dealer, generally limiting possession to ten days’ supply. It makes the Kwantung Monopoly Bureau responsible for distributing opium and manufacturing prepared and medicinal opium, while regulating medical, experimental, and retail access. Dealers must buy from the monopoly, sell only to designated permit holders, keep detailed records, and report monthly to police. The final articles establish business sanctions, imprisonment, fines, and derivative responsibility for employees, representatives, and juridical persons.

subfiles.title: Opium Addiction in the Kwantung Leased Territory
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, American consul, Dairen
subfiles.about: Reports the Kwantung government’s official count of permitted opium smokers.
subfiles.summary: Turner supplements his March 24 monopoly report with information supplied by the Kwantung government. As of its April 6 note, 28,197 addicts held police permits to smoke opium in the territory.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Kwantung opium-control ordinances and package photographs
subfiles.about: Forwards Turner’s monopoly report, translated ordinances, and photostats of an opium tube and carton to the Commissioner of Narcotics.
subfiles.summary: The Department sends Dairen despatch No. 9 and translations of Imperial Ordinance No. 84 and Kwantung Bureau Ordinance No. 8 under the Narcotic Drugs Import and Export Act. It highlights the penalties for retail dealers who manufacture or adulterate prepared opium. Because the Department lacks Imperial Ordinances Nos. 389 of 1934 and 7 of 1937, it has requested copies and translations from Dairen.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment and request for earlier Kwantung opium ordinances
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: William T. Turner, American consul, Dairen
subfiles.about: Commends Turner’s report and requests copies and translations of the 1934 and 1937 amendments.
subfiles.summary: The Department rates Turner’s March 24 report “Very Good” and plans to send a copy to the American representative on the Opium Advisory Committee at Geneva. It requests five copies and translations of Imperial Ordinances No. 389 of 1934 and No. 7 of 1937.

subfiles.title: Transmitting Opium Control Law
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, American consul, Dairen
subfiles.about: Supplies translations of the requested 1934 and 1937 amendments to the Kwantung Opium Ordinance.
subfiles.summary: Turner complies with the April 29 instruction by forwarding translations of Imperial Ordinance No. 389—not No. 380—of December 26, 1934, and Imperial Ordinance No. 7 of February 1, 1937. He describes both enactments as self-explanatory.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 389 of December 26, 1934
subfiles.from: Japanese government; translated by William T. Turner
subfiles.about: Transfers powers under the Kwantung Opium Ordinance from the governor to the Japanese ambassador to Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: The amendment replaces references to the Governor of Kwantung with the Ambassador Plenipotentiary to Manchukuo in several articles. It takes effect upon promulgation.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 7 of February 1, 1937
subfiles.from: Japanese government; translated by William T. Turner
subfiles.about: Creates severe penalties for causing or assisting minors to smoke, possess, or transfer opium.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance provides up to seven years’ penal servitude or a ¥5,000 fine for using force or persuasion to involve persons under twenty-one in opium smoking or unlawful possession and transfer. Aiding or abetting such conduct carries lesser but still substantial penalties. Enforcement was fixed from February 21, 1937.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of 1934 and 1937 Kwantung opium ordinances
subfiles.about: Forwards Turner’s June 6 despatch and translations of Imperial Ordinances Nos. 389 and 7 to the Commissioner of Narcotics.
subfiles.summary: The Department supplies duplicate copies of the Dairen despatch and its two translated legal enclosures. The materials concern control of narcotics traffic in the Kwantung Leased Territory.

subfiles.title: Kwantung Opium Monopoly
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, American consul, Dairen
subfiles.about: Transmits a newspaper report showing continued addiction and argues that monopoly profits discourage decisive suppression.
subfiles.summary: Turner concludes that the stricter laws introduced earlier in 1938 have not reduced addiction and may have coincided with an increase, especially among Japanese residents of Dairen. He reports personally purchasing non-monopoly opium openly at the Ryoto Hotel and a prominent Chinese restaurant, both of which supplied smoking facilities. Turner suggests that rising Japanese addiction might finally spur action where Chinese and Korean suffering did not. He emphasizes that monopoly revenue of about ¥2.2 million formed a large part of a territorial budget of ¥23 million.

subfiles.title: Newspaper report on addiction and the Kwantung Sanitarium
subfiles.about: Reports increasing opium addiction, more than 1,000 registered Japanese addicts in Dairen, and plans for compulsory treatment.
subfiles.summary: The article says compulsory cures and stricter enforcement against dishonest dealers have failed to end addiction, while cold weather has brought more unconscious and dead victims. Dairen alone reportedly has over 1,000 Japanese addicts from all social classes, prompting plans for a blacklist and intensified treatment. Sanitarium chief Sakui says many patients have been treated but warns that unemployed patients commonly relapse.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of despatch on Kwantung addiction and opium revenue
subfiles.about: Forwards Turner’s November 29 despatch and newspaper enclosure concerning addiction levels and monopoly profit.
subfiles.summary: The Department sends duplicate copies of despatch No. 60 and its enclosure to the Treasury Department. An additional copy is provided to the Public Health Service because the report concerns both the extent of addiction and the fiscal profit from opium sales.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Kwantung opium-trade statistics
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch presenting statistics from Statistics of Trade in the Kwantung Territory, 1937.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references file 893.11416 Manchuria/341. It identifies a May 8, 1939 Dairen despatch based on a Kwantung Bureau publication issued at Hoinking.

subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting Japanese shipboard opium-transport regulations
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle, Jr., American ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits a translation of Japanese Communications Department Ordinance No. 5 governing opium transportation aboard Japanese ships.
subfiles.summary: Castle forwards the regulation as published in the Official Gazette of March 17, 1930. The enclosure establishes when Japanese vessels may lawfully transport opium and what reporting duties apply.

subfiles.title: Ordinance No. 5: Rules Relating to Transportation of Opium on Ships
subfiles.from: Matajiro Koizumi, Japanese minister of communications
subfiles.about: Regulates authorized opium carriage by Japanese ships, requires detailed reports for foreign transport, and sets penalties for violations.
subfiles.summary: Japanese ships may carry opium only when authorized between specified Japanese territories, lawfully engaged in international import or export, or compliant with relevant domestic laws abroad. Captains carrying opium in foreign trade must report vessel, owner, captain, cargo, ports, dates, shippers, and consignees through the Japanese consulate and attach proof of legality. Violations carry imprisonment or fines, and the final provisions extend liability to legal representatives, corporate representatives, supervisors, charterers, and acting captains.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Japanese opium-shipping ordinance to Treasury
subfiles.about: Forwards the Tokyo embassy despatch and translation of Ordinance No. 5 for Treasury information.
subfiles.summary: The State Department refers to its March 15 correspondence and transmits a copy of despatch No. 72 with the Japanese shipping regulation. The ordinance had appeared in the March 17 Official Gazette.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Japanese opium-shipping ordinance to Commerce
subfiles.about: Forwards the Tokyo embassy despatch and translation of Ordinance No. 5 for Commerce Department information.
subfiles.summary: This parallel transmittal sends Commerce a copy of despatch No. 72 and its translated regulation. The subject is control of opium transportation aboard Japanese vessels.

subfiles.title: Inquiry concerning cocaine advertisements reported in the Washington Herald
subfiles.about: Requests the name and date of the Japanese trade paper allegedly advertising hundreds of tons of cocaine for sale in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Caldwell quotes the opening of Kenneth Clark’s April 29 Washington Herald article, which reproduced advertisements purporting to offer 100 and 1,000 tons or more of cocaine at Tokyo. He asks whether the quotations came from Treasury Department material and seeks the trade paper’s title and issue date. Caldwell explains that State Department representatives in Japan need these details to conduct an effective investigation.

subfiles.title: Sales of Dope Advertised by Paper in Japan
subfiles.about: Claims that a Japanese trade paper advertised enormous quantities of cocaine and describes worldwide illicit-drug routes.
subfiles.summary: The article reproduces two purported advertisements offering 100 tons and up to 1,000 or 1,800 tons of cocaine in Tokyo, quantities said to exceed legitimate world requirements for generations. It alleges large-scale trafficking through Shanghai and Xiamen and onward to India, the Straits Settlements, Canada, and the United States. It also accuses factories in France and Switzerland of supplying Egypt and describes flows of opium and cocaine involving China, British India, and Japanese-marked contraband.
